Criterion A: Planning:
# Criterion A: Planning
## What it assesses
Criterion A: Planning assesses how you set up the project. You state a learning goal for the project and explain the connection between the goal and personal interests; state an intended product and develop appropriate success criteria for it; and present a detailed plan for achieving the product.

## How to do well
Make the learning goal specific and challenging. Write success criteria that are measurable. Use a timeline with milestones.

## How it is assessed
Each MYP criterion is marked from 0 to 8 using level descriptors, which describe what work looks like at each band. Command terms such as outline, explain, analyse and evaluate show the depth required. Teachers judge the best fit across the strands of the criterion.

## Key terms
Learning goal: what you want to learn through the project
Success criteria: measurable standards for the product
Milestone: a key point in the project timeline
Level descriptor: a description of what work looks like at each band
Command term: a word that shows the depth of answer required
Criterion B: Applying skills:
# Criterion B: Applying skills
## What it assesses
Criterion B: Applying skills assesses how you use approaches to learning (ATL) skills. You explain how you applied ATL skills to achieve your learning goal, and how you applied ATL skills to achieve your product.

## How to do well
Give specific examples of thinking, research, self-management, communication and social skills from your process journal, with evidence.

## How it is assessed
Each MYP criterion is marked from 0 to 8 using level descriptors, which describe what work looks like at each band. Command terms such as outline, explain, analyse and evaluate show the depth required. Teachers judge the best fit across the strands of the criterion.

## Key terms
ATL skills: approaches to learning: thinking, research, self-management, communication and social skills
Self-management: organizing time and work
Evidence: extracts that show what you did
Level descriptor: a description of what work looks like at each band
Command term: a word that shows the depth of answer required
Criterion C: Reflecting:
# Criterion C: Reflecting
## What it assesses
Criterion C: Reflecting assesses reflection on the project. You explain the impact of the project on yourself or your learning, and evaluate the product based on the success criteria.

## How to do well
Explain how the project changed your knowledge, skills or attitudes. Judge the product against each success criterion honestly, with evidence.

## How it is assessed
Each MYP criterion is marked from 0 to 8 using level descriptors, which describe what work looks like at each band. Command terms such as outline, explain, analyse and evaluate show the depth required. Teachers judge the best fit across the strands of the criterion.

## Key terms
Impact: how the project changed you or your learning
Evaluation: judging the product against success criteria
Reflection: thinking about what you learned
Level descriptor: a description of what work looks like at each band
Command term: a word that shows the depth of answer required
Choosing a learning goal and product:
# Choosing a learning goal and product
## Learning goal and product
The personal project is a student-led project completed in the final year of the MYP. A learning goal is what you want to learn, such as how to code a game or how to cook healthy meals. A product is the outcome you create to show that learning, such as a website, a model, a performance or an event.

## Choosing well
Choose a topic you care about and that stretches you. Link it to a global context. Make sure the product is achievable with your time and resources. Write success criteria that describe what a high-quality product looks like.

## Key terms
Personal project: a student-led project in the last year of the MYP
Product: the outcome created in the personal project
Global context: one of six real-world settings for learning in the MYP
Achievable: possible with the time and resources available
The process journal:
# The process journal
## The process journal
The process journal is a record of your personal project from start to finish. It can include notes, brainstorms, research, timelines, photos, drafts and reflections. It is not assessed directly, but extracts from it are used as evidence in the report.

## Using it well
Write regularly, at least once a week. Record decisions and the reasons for them. Note the ATL skills you use. Keep track of sources in a bibliography. Reflect on problems and how you solved them.

## Key terms
Process journal: a record of your project from start to finish
Extract: a selected piece of the process journal used as evidence
Brainstorm: a quick collection of ideas
Bibliography: a list of sources used
The final report:
# The final report
## The report
The final report presents your personal project and is assessed against criteria A, B and C. It is a written report of up to 15 pages, or an oral or multimedia presentation of up to 15 minutes, with up to 10 process journal extracts as evidence.

## Writing it
Organize the report by criterion: planning, applying skills and reflecting. Include your learning goal, product, success criteria, plan, evidence of ATL skills, evaluation and impact. Cite sources and include an academic honesty form. Academic honesty means presenting your own work and acknowledging the work of others.

## Key terms
Final report: the assessed presentation of the personal project
Academic honesty: presenting your own work and acknowledging others
Evidence: extracts that support your claims
Report structure: organizing the report by criterion
